rationale: A leaf-extract Parkinson model measured neuron histology and a separate leaf-oil seizure study reported motor impairment. Neither comparison measured stride length after culinary intake.
Bay-leaf extracts and constituents affected gastric physiology in ethanol studies. No primary record measured levodopa exposure or daily OFF duration after ground leaf.
Rodent essential-oil sedation and reduced responsiveness after infant infusion are distinct from dreaming. No REM sleep or dream-enactment count was retrieved.
New oral leads describe acute infant drooling after concentrated decoction and salivary weight after an extract tablet. Neither measured ground bay leaf and Parkinson drooling severity.

Injectable leaf fraction was studied with neuronal histology in a Parkinson model. Mouse motor impairment and rat exploratory activity were recorded in other models without gait speed after ground bay leaf.

A patent-reported trial of oral extract in healthy adults found lower constipation ratings within the extract arm and gave no between-arm test. Injected aqueous extract slowed rat intestinal transit. The ground leaf claim in Parkinson constipation remains unresolved.
A whole-leaf infusion trial measured anxiety and stress, and an inhalation experiment measured task and mood outcomes. Neither assessed motivation or clinical apathy in Parkinson’s.
A lower inhaled exposure preserved late vigilance in healthy students and an animal study measured memory after incense. The effect of consuming ground bay leaf on Parkinson attention is unmeasured.

One adult had fatigue during probable liver injury after prolonged oral tea consumption. A healthy-participant inhalation study measured vigilance. No comparable ground-leaf Parkinson fatigue scale was found.
